newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-RUSSIAN SEASON ENDS ON HIGH, BUT TROUBLES NOT OVER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RUSSIAN SEASON ENDS ON HIGH, BUT TROUBLES NOT OVER.

text.p: Spartak Moscow have landed their fourth Russian championship in five years but the compelling climax to the league title battle cannot hide problems facing the country's soccer.
Spartak triumphed with a 2-1 playoff victory over 1995 champions Alania Vladikavkaz on Saturday -- a finale any league would have been proud of.
A goal apiece in the last 10 minutes kept millions of television viewers on edge in a way to please those FIFA officials who fear the sport is too dull for the MTV generation.

Yet the excitement of the showdown in St Petersburg, which saw the capital's stylish aristocrats finally get the better of the muscular provincial upstarts from the North Caucasus, will do little to assuage the self-doubt that has gripped Russian football since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Money, or the lack of it, is a recurrent theme. The lure of west European riches has drained the Russian league of talent.
Attendances have slumped embarrassingly low. And this season has seen an upsurge of English-style hooliganism.

The national side was one of the biggest disappointments of Euro '96 and the 1994 World Cup. And not a single club side is left in this year's European competitions, perhaps due partly to playing in a season out of synch with the rest of the continent.
Alania's 7-2 humiliation at home to Glasgow Rangers in the European Cup underscored the Russian league's fragility.
The loss of such clubs as Ukraine's Dynamo Kiev and Georgia's Dynamo Tbilisi has unduly concentrated soccer power in Moscow.
As winter sets in and the Russian close season of frozen, snow-covered pitches begins, there are some bright spots.
Not least, was the dramatic end to the 1996 season.
Five clubs, including Alania and Rotor Volgograd from outside the capital, were in the running until the final fortnight. The playoff was watched by millions on television.
The national side have put failure in England behind them and sit comfortably at the top of their World Cup qualifying group.
League statistics show a slight upturn in attendances.

But it will take more than the sell-out 25,000 crowd in St Petersburg on Saturday to make up for echoingly empty stands the rest of the season. Even with seats typically costing just $2, average premier league attendance is around 10,000.
Signs of a new wave of close-season exile has already begun.
Dmitry Cheryshev, whose 17 goals for Dynamo Moscow made him the league's third top scorer this season, was set to play his first game for Spain's Sporting Gijon on Sunday.

Goals against Alania from international stars Andrei Tikhonov and Ilya Tsymbalar, respectively Russia's Player of the Year and runner-up, may have been their last for the club if western scouts inflict the same damage on Spartak as last year.
Coach Georgy Yartsev had to rebuild his team when Viktor Onopko, Yuri Nikiforov and Sergei Yuran left for the West after securing Spartak full points in last year's European Cup Champions' League.
A growing hunger for success is, however, starting to draw some of Russia's new money to the game and prompt other changes.

Torpedo Moscow, whose players went unpaid when the team's ZiL car plant owners ran into money troubles, are to move into the newly covered-in 100,000-seat Luzhniki Stadium. And the club's cash-rich new owners say they are ready to spend.

Moves are also afoot to bring the season into line with the rest of Europe. The league rejected the move last month. But top clubs still hope a final decision in January could overturn that and end what they see is one of their major disadvantages.
